question: Can the spline expressivity attributed to Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks be reproduced by an MLP-like architecture using powers of ReLU and a basis-function shortcut, while avoiding recursive B-spline evaluation?

key_findings.claim: PowerMLP replaces edge-wise recursive B-splines with node-wise ReLU-k activations plus a SiLU-like basis-function branch.
key_findings.evidence: Each nonfinal layer computes alpha times b(x) plus sigma_k(Wx+gamma), where sigma_k(x)=max(0,x)^k and b(x)=x/(1+exp(-x)); the final layer is affine. A classical truncated-power identity expresses each B-spline as a linear combination of shifted ReLU-k functions, avoiding the de Boor-Cox recursion used by the compared KAN implementation.

anchors.section: 4.2 Lemma 1: representing B-splines with powers of ReLU

key_findings.claim: The paper proves mutual exact representability on bounded input boxes, but with architecture and parameter transformations rather than a same-size equivalence.
key_findings.evidence: Theorem 2 maps a depth-d, width-w, grid-G KAN into a widened PowerMLP. Theorem 6 maps a depth-d PowerMLP into a depth-2d, width-2w, grid-2 KAN with O(kp) nonzero parameters on [-E,E]^n. Corollary 7 therefore equates represented function sets only on a fixed bounded box and after resource expansion.

key_findings.claim: The claimed strict function-class advantage over KAN on all of R^n is not fully justified by the one-sentence compact-support argument.
key_findings.evidence: Corollary 3 argues that splines vanish outside their knot interval while PowerMLPs contain polynomials. However, the paper's own KAN definition adds a noncompact basis branch u b(x) to every spline activation, so compact support of the spline term alone does not characterize the complete KAN function class. The inclusion is proved, but the cited reasoning does not by itself prove strictness for that residual-basis KAN definition.

key_findings.claim: The analytic FLOP model predicts KAN evaluation to be more than ten times as expensive per parameter in the paper's practical grid regime.
key_findings.evidence: With arithmetic operations counted as one FLOP and comparisons as zero, the derived per-layer formulas make the KAN FLOP-to-parameter ratio exceed 20 for k>=3 and G>=3, while MLP and PowerMLP tend below 2. The matched-small example has 564 FLOPs for a 24-parameter KAN, 36 for a 25-parameter MLP, and 40 for a 25-parameter PowerMLP.

key_findings.claim: Function-fitting results usually favor PowerMLP at matched parameter counts, but the paper's case count is internally inconsistent and uncertainty is omitted.
key_findings.evidence: Table 2 displays 15 named special-function rows and two size regimes, while the text calls them 16 cases and reports PowerMLP wins in 11/10 of 16. The appendix says each network is trained on seeds 42, 114, and 514, but the table provides one value per cell without dispersion or explaining whether it is a mean or selected run.

anchors.section: Appendix B.1 AI for Science tasks

key_findings.claim: The reported approximately forty-fold training speedup is large but benchmark-specific and partly reflects implementation choices.
key_findings.evidence: Across eight full-batch tasks on one RTX 4090, ten timing repetitions give PowerMLP times near MLP and about 40 times below the Python KAN 0.2.5 implementation; for example, KAN versus PowerMLP is 17.73 versus 0.738 seconds on JE and 89.82 versus 2.39 seconds on SVHN. The test does not compare optimized kernels, memory traffic, backward FLOPs, compilation, or equal wall-clock accuracy.

key_findings.claim: Accuracy comparisons do not use symmetric model-selection protocols.
key_findings.evidence: The appendix states that KAN uses the default configuration from the original KAN paper, whereas MLP and PowerMLP use Adam, a modified warm-up schedule, and grid search over ten learning rates from 1e-4 to 1e-1. Selecting the better rate only for two model families can contribute to their apparent accuracy and convergence advantage.

key_findings.claim: PowerMLP is not uniformly superior to ordinary MLPs or robust at high polynomial order.
key_findings.evidence: The main classification summary says PowerMLP loses to MLP on MNIST and SVHN. Supplementary CNN/RNN substitutions yield only small improvements, and fifth-order PowerMLP fails to converge on every tried CIFAR-10 seed. The authors also identify complicated vision and long-text processing as limitations without convolution or attention structure.

method.core_idea: Compile finite-grid B-spline activations into shifted ReLU-power units inside a familiar MLP-style layer and retain KAN's nonparametric basis shortcut.
method.mechanism: A divided-difference identity converts each order-k B-spline into k+2 shifted ReLU-k terms. Layerwise substitution proves KAN-to-PowerMLP inclusion; a two-layer spline construction for affine maps, ReLU-k, and the basis addition gives the reverse bounded-domain inclusion. Analytic operation counts and matched-parameter experiments compare the compiled network with KAN and ReLU MLPs.
assumptions: KAN knots are distinct where the truncated-power identity divides by knot differences.
The reverse representation is needed only on a known bounded input box.
ReLU exponentiation and the fixed basis branch are numerically stable at the chosen order and scale.
Simple scalar FLOP counts predict actual framework and hardware latency.
Matched parameter count and depth constitute a fair capacity comparison despite different tuning protocols.

techniques.role: Expresses each finite-grid B-spline as shifted powers of ReLU without recursion.
Adds a trainable fixed-basis shortcut to an affine ReLU-k MLP layer.
Constructively converts PowerMLP layers to two KAN layers and KAN activations to PowerMLP units.
Compares arithmetic operation counts after approximately matching trainable parameter totals.
Tests special functions, knot signatures, tabular data, TF-IDF text, and flattened images.

evaluations.setting: Special-function regression at roughly 25 and 700 parameters over three listed seeds
evaluations.result: PowerMLP is reported best in 11 small-size and 10 large-size cases, although the table displays 15 rows while the text uses a denominator of 16.
evaluations.baseline: KAN 0.2.5 and ReLU MLP with approximately matched parameter counts

evaluations.result: PowerMLP identifies the same three relevant invariants and reaches 86.74% with all three; it outperforms the cited KAN result on three of four multi-input combinations.
evaluations.baseline: Original MLP discovery experiment and KAN reproduction

evaluations.setting: Titanic, Income, SMS Spam, AG News, MNIST, and grayscale SVHN
evaluations.result: PowerMLP beats matched KAN on all six plotted tasks, beats MLP on tabular/text tasks, and trails MLP on both image tasks.
evaluations.baseline: Approximately parameter-matched KAN and MLP of the same depth

evaluations.setting: Eight full-batch timing tasks on one RTX 4090, ten repetitions
evaluations.result: PowerMLP averages roughly 40 times faster than the compared KAN implementation and remains close to MLP timing.
evaluations.baseline: KAN 0.2.5 and MLP under the paper's timing protocol

evaluations.metric: Test RMSE across depth or parameter count
evaluations.result: Removing the basis branch destabilizes deeper networks, while replacing ReLU-k with ReLU worsens every plotted configuration.
evaluations.baseline: Full PowerMLP, no-basis PowerMLP, and no-ReLU-k variant

evaluations.setting: PowerMLP substituted into a small VGG on CIFAR-10 and a two-layer-LSTM RNN on CoLA
evaluations.result: Changes are modest; higher orders help up to a point, while order five fails on all tried CIFAR-10 seeds.
evaluations.baseline: Unmodified VGG or RNN MLP component

limitations: Exact reverse equivalence is confined to a fixed bounded domain and expands depth, width, and parameters.
The strict global function-class claim is not established by the compact-support argument given for the residual-basis KAN definition.
Accuracy tuning favors MLP and PowerMLP with a ten-rate search while KAN uses defaults.
Reported tables omit confidence intervals and contain a 15-versus-16 case-count discrepancy.
The FLOP abstraction omits memory movement, automatic-differentiation cost, optimized kernels, and hardware utilization.
Powers of ReLU can create exploding activations and poor conditioning at high order.
The paper does not preserve or evaluate KAN's claimed edge-function interpretability.
Image and long-text experiments require specialized convolutional or attention components for competitive performance.
failure_modes: Inputs leave the interval used to compile a PowerMLP into a KAN, invalidating exact equivalence.
High-order activations overflow or create extreme gradients after modest affine rescaling.
A chosen basis branch dominates the polynomial branch and defeats the intended spline correspondence.
Learning-rate selection rather than architecture explains an apparent convergence advantage.
A theoretically low-FLOP graph runs slowly because generic power operations or small matrix kernels underutilize hardware.
Parameter matching hides a large difference in effective basis count, width, or optimization geometry.
Replacing an MLP block in a specialized architecture yields negligible gains because surrounding layers dominate.
reusable_insights: Compile recursively evaluated bases into closed-form activation expansions before redesigning an entire architecture.
State domain and resource blowups whenever two neural function classes are called equivalent.
Benchmark model families with the same hyperparameter-search budget and report all seeds.
Pair analytic FLOPs with optimized forward/backward throughput and equal-accuracy wall time.
Audit whether an expressivity proof applies to the full residual activation, not just one component.
Stress-test ReLU-power networks under input scaling and high activation order.
open_questions: Is Corollary 3's strict global inclusion true for KANs that retain the noncompact SiLU basis branch?
Can PowerMLP preserve the sparse symbolic interpretability claimed for learned edge splines?
How do optimized fused KAN and PowerMLP kernels compare at equal validation quality on modern accelerators?
Which normalization or parameterization prevents high-order ReLU-power instability?
Do gains survive a nested, equal-budget hyperparameter and architecture search?
What approximation rates distinguish PowerMLP, KAN, and ordinary RePU MLPs at a fixed computational budget?

competitive_landscape.title: KAN: Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks
competitive_landscape.difference: KAN learns edge-wise spline activations and emphasizes accuracy and symbolic interpretability. PowerMLP compiles those spline terms into node-wise ReLU powers for speed, but does not demonstrate the same interpretability workflow.

competitive_landscape.title: Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks are Radial Basis Function Networks
competitive_landscape.difference: FastKAN approximates cubic B-splines with Gaussian radial basis functions while retaining a KAN-like layer. PowerMLP uses an exact truncated-power identity and an MLP-like graph, trading local RBF behavior for polynomial ReLU units.

competitive_landscape.title: BSRBF-KAN: A combination of B-splines and Radial Basis Functions in Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks
competitive_landscape.difference: BSRBF-KAN blends splines and RBFs and benchmarks EfficientKAN, FastKAN, FasterKAN, and related variants over repeated image-classification runs. PowerMLP presents stronger representation theorems and broader tasks but a less symmetric tuning protocol.

competitive_landscape.title: On the Expressiveness and Spectral Bias of KANs
competitive_landscape.difference: The ICLR 2025 paper proves MLP-to-KAN and KAN-to-MLP simulations and studies spectral bias and grid extension. PowerMLP adds a concrete basis-augmented ReLU-power implementation and speed benchmarks, while its bounded-domain equivalence overlaps the theoretical comparison.

competitive_landscape.title: Kolmogorov-Arnold Convolutions: Design Principles and Empirical Studies
competitive_landscape.difference: This work builds parameter-efficient KAN convolution, attention, and segmentation components and evaluates much richer vision suites. PowerMLP is simpler and faster as a generic MLP replacement but acknowledges that its plain form is weak on complicated vision tasks.

novelty_assessment: PowerMLP's useful engineering idea is an exact, nonrecursive truncated-power compilation of spline terms into a basis-augmented RePU-style MLP, accompanied by constructive bounded-domain conversions and broad timing tests. ReLU-power networks, FastKAN variants, and mutual KAN/MLP representation results already existed or were concurrent, so the novelty lies in this particular architecture and packaging. The empirical speed claim is credible for the tested PyTorch implementations; the strict global expressivity and architecture-level superiority claims are materially less secure.
reviewer_notes: Read all 14 extracted pages, including full proofs, experiment details, tuning protocol, supplemental CNN/RNN studies, and failure at order five. Primary arXiv/OpenReview records for KAN, FastKAN, BSRBF-KAN, KAN expressiveness/spectral bias, and KAN convolutions were checked on 2026-08-23. The review explicitly separates exact function representation from equal-resource approximation, optimization, latency, and interpretability.
